bib.title: Clean Code, Chapter 11: Systems
bib.venue: Robert C. Martin, Clean Code: A Handbook of Agile Software Craftsmanship, Prentice Hall (chapter 11, pp. 153-169)

question: How do we keep a software system clean at the system level, above the code level?

results.claim: Software systems should separate startup (construction and wiring of objects) from runtime logic.
results.setup: Clean Code ch. 11, Java systems, 2008 (Java 5, Spring 2.5, EJB2/3)
results.quote:
Software systems should separate the startup process, when the application objects are
constructed and the dependencies are “wired” together, from the runtime logic that takes
over after startup.

results.claim: Lazy initialization hard-codes a dependency, forces test doubles, and breaks SRP in a small way.
results.setup: Clean Code ch. 11, Java systems, 2008 (Java 5, Spring 2.5, EJB2/3)
results.quote:
Having both of these responsibilities means that the method is doing more than one thing, so we are breaking the Single Responsibility Principle
in a small way.

results.claim: Separation of Main: all construction in main, dependencies point one way, away from main.
results.setup: Clean Code ch. 11, Java systems, 2008 (Java 5, Spring 2.5, EJB2/3)
results.quote:
They
all go one direction, pointing away from main.

results.claim: Dependency Injection is IoC applied to dependency management; the class is passive and exposes setters or constructor arguments.
results.setup: Clean Code ch. 11, Java systems, 2008 (Java 5, Spring 2.5, EJB2/3)
results.quote:
The class takes no direct steps to
resolve its dependencies; it is completely passive.

results.claim: Lazy instantiation is just an optimization and perhaps premature.
results.setup: Clean Code ch. 11, Java systems, 2008 (Java 5, Spring 2.5, EJB2/3)
results.quote: Don’t forget that lazy instantiation/evaluation is just an optimization and perhaps premature!

results.claim: It is a myth that systems can be got right first time; implement today's stories and refactor.
results.setup: Clean Code ch. 11, Java systems, 2008 (Java 5, Spring 2.5, EJB2/3)
results.quote: It is a myth that we can get systems “right the ﬁrst time.”

results.claim: Software architecture can grow incrementally if concerns are separated.
results.setup: Clean Code ch. 11, Java systems, 2008 (Java 5, Spring 2.5, EJB2/3)
results.quote:
Their architectures can grow
incrementally, if we maintain the proper separation of concerns.

results.claim: EJB2 coupled business logic to the container, making unit testing and reuse hard.
results.setup: Clean Code ch. 11, Java systems, 2008 (Java 5, Spring 2.5, EJB2/3)
results.quote: The business logic is tightly coupled to the EJB2 application “container.”

results.claim: Cross-cutting concerns (persistence, transactions, security) cut across domain objects; AOP restores their modularity.
results.setup: Clean Code ch. 11, Java systems, 2008 (Java 5, Spring 2.5, EJB2/3)
results.quote:
We use the term cross-cutting concerns for concerns like
these.

results.claim: JDK proxies are verbose, work only on interfaces and give no system-wide points of interest, so they make clean code hard.
results.setup: Clean Code ch. 11, Java systems, 2008 (Java 5, Spring 2.5, EJB2/3)
results.quote:
They make it hard to create clean
code!

results.claim: Spring AOP / JBoss AOP (pure Java) cover most uses of aspects; AspectJ adds power at the cost of new tools and language.
results.quote: ﬁcient for 80–90 percent of the cases where aspects are most useful.
results.note: Unsupported estimate by Wampler; no source.

results.claim: Spring decorators ('Russian doll'): client calls the outermost of nested decorator objects around a POJO.
results.setup: Clean Code ch. 11, Java systems, 2008 (Java 5, Spring 2.5, EJB2/3)
results.quote:
The client believes it is invoking getAccounts() on a Bank object, but it is actually talk-
ing to the outermost of a set of nested DECORATOR14 objects
results.note: Hyphenated across lines in source: 'talk-ing'. Full wording: 'talking to the outermost of a set of nested DECORATOR objects'.

results.claim: With POJO domain logic you can test drive the architecture; Big Design Up Front is harmful.
results.setup: Clean Code ch. 11, Java systems, 2008 (Java 5, Spring 2.5, EJB2/3)
results.quote:
BDUF is even
harmful because it inhibits adapting to change

results.claim: Optimal architecture: modularized domains of POJOs integrated with minimally invasive aspects, test-driven like code.
results.setup: Clean Code ch. 11, Java systems, 2008 (Java 5, Spring 2.5, EJB2/3)
results.quote:
This architecture can
be test-driven, just like the code.

results.claim: Postpone decisions until the last possible moment; a premature decision is made with suboptimal knowledge.
results.setup: Clean Code ch. 11, Java systems, 2008 (Java 5, Spring 2.5, EJB2/3)
results.quote: it is also best to postpone decisions until the last possible moment.

results.claim: Use standards only when they add demonstrable value; EJB2 was adopted because it was a standard.
results.setup: Clean Code ch. 11, Java systems, 2008 (Java 5, Spring 2.5, EJB2/3)
results.quote:
Many teams used the EJB2 architecture because it was a standard, even when lighter-
weight and more straightforward designs would have been sufﬁcient.

results.claim: A good DSL minimizes the communication gap between domain concept and code.
results.setup: Clean Code ch. 11, Java systems, 2008 (Java 5, Spring 2.5, EJB2/3)
results.quote:
A good DSL minimizes the “communication gap” between a domain concept and the
code that implements it

results.claim: Conclusion: use the simplest thing that can possibly work, at system and module level.
results.setup: Clean Code ch. 11, Java systems, 2008 (Java 5, Spring 2.5, EJB2/3)
results.quote:
never forget to use the
simplest thing that can possibly work.

limits: Java-specific (EJB2/3, Spring 2.5, JDK proxies, AspectJ); 2008 tooling has dated.
Claims are argued by analogy (cities, buildings) and anecdote, no measurements.
The 80-90 percent figure for pure-Java AOP is an unsourced estimate.
Chapter is by Kevin Dean Wampler, not Martin, in a book credited to Martin.
practices: Move all construction and wiring to main or modules it calls, and design the rest assuming objects are built (Separation of Main, p. 155).
Use an Abstract Factory when the application must control when an object is created (p. 156).
Use Dependency Injection: classes take dependencies by constructor or setter and do not resolve them (p. 157).
Implement only today's stories, then refactor and expand (p. 158).
Write domain logic as POJOs and add cross-cutting concerns with aspect-like mechanisms (pp. 163, 167).
Avoid Big Design Up Front; start with a naively simple but decoupled architecture (p. 167).
Postpone decisions until the last possible moment (p. 168).
Use standards wisely, when they add demonstrable value (p. 168).
Use domain-specific languages to close the gap between domain and code (pp. 168-169).
Use the simplest thing that can possibly work (p. 169).

terms.definition: concerns like persistence that tend to cut across the natural object boundaries of a domain
the application of Inversion of Control (IoC) to dependency management
Plain Old Java Object, purely focused on its domain with no dependencies on enterprise frameworks
the practice of designing everything up front before implementing anything at all
separate, small scripting languages or APIs in standard languages that permit code to be written so that it reads like a structured form of prose that a domain expert might write
